```text
24	We characterize a \emph{differential depth response} in distributional features computed under a held-out reference model: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy mean, type-token ratio, hapax ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay rate) remain near-stationary.
25	Combining both feature types into a 7-feature ensemble exploits this complementarity: the full set (macro-F1\,=\,0.79) outperforms surface-only (0.73) and reference-only (0.75) subsets.
26	In leave-one-generator-out evaluation across 6 generators from 3 model families (0.6B--8B parameters), the ensemble achieves macro-F1 of 0.79 ($p < 0.001$ vs.\ all single-detector baselines), with per-generator held-out F1 ranging from 0.68 to 0.86.
```

```text
1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Task Formulation}
5	\label{sec:task}
6	
7	Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
8	Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
9	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
10	We frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.
11	Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, as preliminary experiments showed diminishing discriminability at higher depths---consistent with the monotonic convergence of distributional features reported in \S\ref{sec:results}.
12	
13	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
14	\label{sec:generation}
15	
16	We construct generation chains using six generators spanning three model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, and \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}.
17	This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
18	
19	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
20	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
21	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
22	The resulting dataset contains approximately 27{,}000 texts across all generators and depths.
23	For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.
24	
25	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
26	\label{sec:features}
27	
28	We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.
29	
30	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
31	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than and architecturally independent of all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
32	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract four statistics:
33	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
34	    \item \textbf{entropy\_mean}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;
35	    \item \textbf{entropy\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;
36	    \item \textbf{entropy\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;
37	    \item \textbf{tail\_decay}: proportion of tokens whose NLL exceeds the 90th percentile of the reference distribution (computed over $\mathcal{C}_0$), measuring how heavy-tailed the NLL distribution is relative to human text.
38	\end{itemize}
39	
40	\paragraph{Surface features.}
41	Three features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:
42	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
43	    \item \textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);
44	    \item \textbf{hapax\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\emph{hapax legomena});
45	    \item \textbf{entropy\_min}: minimum token-level NLL under the reference model---despite being computed via the reference model, this feature empirically tracks surface-level text properties (extremely predictable tokens) and groups with the surface features in ablation behavior.
46	\end{itemize}
47	
48	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
49	The grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\_mean, TTR, hapax\_ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy\_std, tail\_decay) remain near-stationary.
50	This differential behavior---consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form---motivates combining both feature types.
51	As shown in \S\ref{sec:results}, the full 7-feature set significantly outperforms either group alone.
52	
53	\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
54	\label{sec:evaluation}
55	
56	\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
57	To evaluate generalization to unseen generators, we use \textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation: in each fold, one of the six generators is held out for testing and the remaining five provide training data.
58	We additionally report \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.
59	
60	\paragraph{Classifier.}
61	We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} as the classifier throughout.
62	Gradient-boosted trees handle heterogeneous feature scales and nonlinear interactions without extensive hyperparameter tuning, and their feature importance scores support interpretability.
63	The same hyperparameter configuration is used across all experiments to avoid fold-specific overfitting.
64	
65	\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}
66	The primary metric is \textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes, which weights minority classes (gen-1, gen-2+) equally against the typically easier gen-0 class.
67	We report per-class F1 scores and 95\% bootstrap confidence intervals ($n{=}1{,}000$ resamples).
68	For pairwise model comparisons (e.g., full features vs.\ ablated subsets), we use the \textbf{McNemar test} on disagreement tables.
69	For comparisons against detection baselines, we use \textbf{paired bootstrap} significance tests.
70	All reported $p$-values are two-sided.
71	
72	\paragraph{Baselines.}
73	We compare the 7-feature ensemble against four single-score detection methods repurposed as ordinal depth predictors: Avg-LogProb, FastDetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars}, and LD-Score \cite{ld_score}.
74	Each baseline score is used as a univariate feature in the same XGBoost framework under LOGO cross-validation, ensuring a controlled comparison.
75	
76	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
77	Since TTR and hapax\_ratio are mechanically length-dependent, we verify that depth signal is not an artifact of systematic length variation.
78	We conduct three complementary analyses: (1) Spearman correlation between text length and each feature (requiring $|\rho| < 0.15$ for non-confounded features), (2) classification with length-normalized features, and (3) comparison on length-matched subsets.
79	
```

```json
    "originalFile": "\\section{Method}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\n\\subsection{Task Formulation}\n\\label{sec:task}\n\nGiven a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \\emph{generation depth} $d \\in \\{0, 1, 2{+}\\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.\nFormally, let $\\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.\nA generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \\sim \\mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \\geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.\nWe frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.\nDepths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, as preliminary experiments showed diminishing discriminability at higher depths---consistent with the monotonic convergence of distributional features reported in \\S\\ref{sec:results}.\n\n\\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}\n\\label{sec:generation}\n\nWe construct generation chains using six generators spanning three model families: \\textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \\cite{pythia}, \\textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \\cite{olmo}, and \\textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \\cite{qwen3}.\nThis selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.\n\nFor each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\\mathcal{C}_0$.\nEach seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\\texttt{Continue the following text: \\{text\\}}''.\nAll generation uses temperature $\\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.\nThe resulting dataset contains approximately 27{,}000 texts across all generators and depths.\nFor classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.\n\n\\subsection{Feature Extraction}\n\\label{sec:features}\n\nWe extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.\n\n\\paragraph{Reference-model features.}\nA held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than and architecturally independent of all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.\nFrom the resulting NLL sequence, we extract four statistics:\n\\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]\n    \\item \\textbf{entropy\\_mean}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;\n    \\item \\textbf{entropy\\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;\n    \\item \\textbf{entropy\\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;\n    \\item \\textbf{tail\\_decay}: proportion of tokens text.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\paragraph{Surface features.}\nThree features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:\n\\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]\n    \\item \\textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);\n    \\item \\textbf{hapax\\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\\emph{hapax legomena});\n    \\item \\textbf{entropy\\_min}: minimum token-level NLL under the reference model---despite being computed via the reference model, this feature empirically tracks surface-level text properties (extremely predictable tokens) and groups with the surface features in ablation behavior.\n\\end{itemize}\n\n\\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}\nThe grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \\emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\\_mean, TTR, hapax\\_ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy\\_std, tail\\_decay) remain near-stationary.\nThis differential behavior---consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution while preserving its functional form---motivates combining both feature types.\nAs shown in \\S\\ref{sec:results}, the full 7-feature set significantly outperforms either group alone.\n\n\\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}\n\\label{sec:evaluation}\n\n\\paragraph{Cross-validation.}\nTo evaluate generalization to unseen generators, we use \\textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation: in each fold, one of the six generators is held out for testing and the remaining five provide training data.\nWe additionally report \\textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.\n\n\\paragraph{Classifier.}\nWe use XGBoost \\cite{xgboost} as the classifier throughout.\nGradient-boosted trees handle heterogeneous feature scales and nonlinear interactions without extensive hyperparameter tuning, and their feature importance scores support interpretability.\nThe same hyperparameter configuration is used across all experiments to avoid fold-specific overfitting.\n\n\\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}\nThe primary metric is \\textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes, which weights minority classes (gen-1, gen-2+) equally against the typically easier gen-0 class.\nWe report per-class F1 scores and 95\\% bootstrap confidence intervals ($n{=}1{,}000$   "task_type": "analysis:plan-005-feature-extraction",
```
````json
  "project": "gen-depth-fingerprint",
  "task_prompt": "## 任务：plan-005-cont 特征提取\n\n### 目标\n用 Pythia-410M 参考模型对 plan-005-cont（continuation prompt type）的生成数据提取 7 个深度指纹特征，保存为可直接用于后续分析的格式。\n\n### 环境\n- 服务器：autodl-5090 (root@autodl-5090)\n- GPU：使用 cuda:0\n- 项目路径：/root/gen-depth-fingerprint\n- 环境激活：`source /root/miniconda3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh && conda activate base`\n- SSH 前先：`source /etc/network_turbo`（如果需要下载）\n\n### 数据文件\n- 输入：`/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/data/pythia-2.8b-continuation/generations_shard0.jsonl`\n- 4,620 records, 995 seeds, depth 0-4\n\n### 步骤\n\n1. **SSH 连接，探测现有代码**：\n   ```\n   ls /root/gen-depth-fingerprint/scripts/\n   ls /root/gen-depth-fingerprint/src/\n   ```\n   找到已有的特征提取脚本（之前的实验已经用过特征提取，应该有现成的代码）。\n\n2. **检查 Pythia-410M 模型位置**：\n   ```\n   ls /root/autodl-tmp/.hf_cache/models--EleutherAI--pythia-410m* 2>/dev/null\n   find /root/autodl-tmp -name \"*pythia-410m*\" -type d 2>/dev/null | head -5\n   ```\n\n3. **运行特征提取**：\n   对每条 record 提取 7 个特征：\n   - **Reference-model features**（用 Pythia-410M）: entropy_mean, entropy_std, entropy_max, entropy_min, tail_decay\n   - **Surface features**: ttr, hapax_ratio\n\n   如果已有脚本，直接使用。如果没有，参考项目中已有的特征提取代码写一个。\n\n   输出到：`/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/data/pythia-2.8b-continuation/features.jsonl`\n   每行格式：`{\"seed\": X, \"depth\": Y, \"prompt_type\": \"continuation\", \"entropy_mean\": ..., \"entropy_std\": ..., \"entropy_max\": ..., \"entropy_min\": ..., \"tail_decay\": ..., \"ttr\": ..., \"hapax_ratio\": ...}`\n\n4. **验证**：\n   - 确认输出行数与输入匹配\n   - 抽查几条记录的特征值是否在合理范围\n   - 打印 depth 0 vs depth 4 的均值对比，初步确认 drift pattern\n\n5. **初步分析**：\n   - 计算每个特征与 depth 的 Spearman ρ\n   - 与原有 continuation 数据（plan-001/plan-002 的 Pythia-2.8B 数据）对比，确认一致性\n\n### 产出\n- 特征文件：`/root/gen-depth-fingerprint/data/pythia-2.8b-continuation/features.jsonl`\n- 在完成消息中报告：\n  - 每个特征的 Spearman ρ\n  - depth 0 vs depth 4 均值对比\n  - 与原有数据的一致性判断\n\n### 注意\n- 使用 cuda:0 运行模型推理\n- 如果 Pythia-410M 需要下载，先 `source /etc/network_turbo`\n- tail_decay 的 90th percentile threshold 应从 gen-0 (depth=0) 数据计算",
````
